title: Your sitting
hookLine: bell, posture, breath, a closing wish of metta

cards: Tomorrow morning there's no app, no teacher, nothing but a place to sit. What do you actually do? For twenty days you've learned pieces: the four phrases, the sixteen steps, counting, the visitors.
What helps now is something simple and repeatable, ten minutes or twenty, done most days. Not a performance. Not a test.
Just a habit with a shape to it. Today, you build yours.

teach.b: Here's a simple shape in four parts, drawn from the breathing discourse and from ordinary practice. First, a bell, or any clear beginning.
In a monastery a bell or gong may open the sitting; it marks the line between the rest of your day and this. A phone timer works fine. Second, posture.
The breathing discourse says: sit down, fold the legs crosswise, set the body upright. That's the old ideal; chairs and cushions both work.
What matters is upright without stiffness: a straight back, relaxed shoulders, hands resting, eyes closed or softly lowered.
Third, the breath. Count to ten if the mind is busy. Know the long and the short.
Feel the whole body, kaya. When a visitor comes, name it, and come back. Don't try all sixteen steps at once; pick one and stay with it.
Fourth, close with a wish of metta. Before you open your eyes, offer the phrases: to yourself, to someone you love, to everyone. May all beings be at ease.
Some Buddhists end a sitting this way, sharing whatever good came of it outward. Then the bell again, and back to your day. How long?
Ten minutes is a real sitting, and ten minutes on most days builds what an hour once a month can't: a habit.

Look at the ten days behind you: sixteen steps, long and short, the whole body, joy and ease, the weather of the mind, gladdening, change, counting, the visitors, and now your own sitting. Ten minutes, yours.

how: A daily sitting can take this shape: a bell or clear start, an upright posture, a breath practice, and a closing wish of loving-kindness or dedication of merit.

practice: The bell has just rung: that's your beginning. Set your posture, upright, shoulders soft, hands resting, and take one step of the breath, counting, long and short, or the whole body; when a visitor comes, name it and return.
Near the end, offer the phrases: may I be at ease, may all beings be at ease.

wordCard.voice: Your sitting. Bell, posture, breath, and a closing wish of metta: a practice you can keep.
